answers.reasoning: The only evidence cited is the two etidronate RCTs (ALS, stroke) pooled in the Iwamoto meta-analysis, both from the Sato group whose 33 RCTs Bolland et al. found statistically implausible; nothing in the sources reports an independent etidronate trial, and 'may be unreliable' is not evidence of no effect.

The RR 0.29 (0.10-0.80) rests on the two Sato alendronate trials (stroke, Parkinson's) in the retracted meta-analysis; once those are discarded no source reports alendronate hip-fracture data in this population, and Bolland only impugns the data's integrity rather than testing efficacy.
All three risedronate RCTs in the pooled analysis are Sato-group Japanese trials covered by Bolland's integrity review; removing them leaves no remaining evidence either way.

The class-level conclusion is just the pooled result of the seven Sato trials in the now-retracted Iwamoto meta-analysis; Bolland's finding of 'very large reductions in hip fracture incidence, regardless of intervention' undermines the data's credibility but does not itself demonstrate that oral bisphosphonates fail to prevent hip fracture.

This statement comes from Fujii's own 2002 review, retracted because the trials underlying its tables and sections 3 and 4.2 were themselves retracted; no non-Fujii PONV evidence appears anywhere in these four sources, so the claim loses its support without acquiring any counter-evidence.

Same provenance problem: the 5-HT3-plus-traditional-antiemetic comparisons are drawn from the Fujii trials the retraction notice names (references 25-29, 31, 32, 47, 48, 50-54), and nothing in the remaining sources speaks to the comparison.

In the source this is stated only as a hypothesis ('There is a possibility that a combination... would be more effective'), and every trial Fujii offered in its support is retracted; a plausible mechanism with no surviving trial evidence is unresolved, not refuted.

The safety statement rests on the same Fujii dataset; the review's own warning about 'additive central nervous system toxicity' concerns combinations of two traditional antiemetics, not a 5-HT3 antagonist plus another agent, so it does not argue against this particular claim.
